title: To study the self
hookLine: Dogen: to study the way is to study the self, to study the self is to forget the self (Genjokoan)

cards: Someone sits in a small boat, looking at the shore. The trees seem to slide past. The dock drifts away.

For a moment it really looks as if the land is moving. Then they glance down at the water against the hull, and it's obvious: the boat is what moves. Dogen uses this picture in a short essay called Genjokoan.
When we look at the world with a confused idea of ourselves, he says, we get the movement backward.

teach.h: STUDY THE WAY: STUDY THE SELF.
teach.b: Here is the heart of it, in plain words. Dogen writes, roughly: to study the Buddha way is to study the self.

teach.h: STUDY THE SELF: FORGET THE SELF.
teach.b: To study the self is to forget the self. To forget the self is to be confirmed by all things. One step at a time.
First, the path isn't a subject out there, like geography. What you're studying is the one doing the studying: how your attention moves, what you grab, what you flinch from. Second, the surprise.
Look closely enough at the self and it stops being the solid thing at the center of everything. Forgetting here isn't amnesia or self-hatred.

It's closer to being so absorbed in kneading bread or fixing a bike chain that the little narrator who comments on everything goes quiet. Third, once the narrator steps back, the world isn't scenery sliding past you.
The dough, the chain, the sound of the street show up fully, and you're part of what's happening instead of watching from a booth.

teach.h: FORGET THE SELF: ALL THINGS CONFIRM.
teach.b: That's the boat again: a self that thinks it's standing still while everything else moves has the picture upside down. Dogen adds that even the traces of awakening are left behind, not held onto.
Readers have worked on these lines for a long time, and they don't all read them the same way.
But the sequence is clear on the page: study, forget, be confirmed.

how: Zen students study the Genjokoan with teachers and in study groups, and some temples chant or read it aloud; teachers often point students back to it during sitting retreats.

p: is to be confirmed by all things
what's really moving, not the shore

the shore seems to move until you look at the boat.

the one studying is the thing being studied.

games.q: you're in a boat and the shore seems to slide away. what does Dogen say to do?
o: close your eyes until it stops
games.why: look at the boat, and you see it's the boat that moves: our picture of the self gets things backward.

practice: For a few minutes, let breathing be the one task you forget yourself in: feel the breath arrive at the nose, fill the chest, and leave.

Each time the narrator starts up, how am I doing, what's next, don't fight it; just hand the attention back to the breath, the way you'd hand a tool back to someone mid-job. See whether, for a breath or two, there's only breathing.

wordCard.voice: Genjokoan. Dogen's essay teaching that to study the way is to study the self, and to study the self is to forget it. Today's word.

orig.note: Japanese Genjokoan, the essay of Dogen's that holds today's line.

carryVoice: Your line: forget the self. The little narrator can rest. That's day nine hundred ninety-eight.
